blocks.label: Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
blocks.text: VBT is concerned with both the formation of bonds and the shapes of molecules. This method of describing a covalent bond considers a molecule as a combination of atoms.

blocks.head: What VBT Explains
blocks.body: VBT explains three things that VSEPR cannot:
items: Reason for bond formation
Strength of the bond
Direction of the bond

items.title: Bond Formation
items.body: — A covalent bond forms when half-filled orbitals in the valence shells of two atoms with similar energy overlap.

items.title: Overlapping Orbitals
items.body: — Two half-filled orbitals overlap and result in formation of one bond.

items.title: Strength
items.body: — Greater overlap of orbitals → stronger bond. Strength increases with extent of overlapping.

items.title: Direction
items.body: — Covalent bonds are directional. The direction of the bond is determined by the shape and mode of the overlapping orbitals. Bond is in the direction of overlapping.

blocks.label: Sigma (σ) Bond
blocks.text: A sigma bond is formed by the linear overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms. The orbitals approach each other on the nuclear axis.

blocks.head: s-s Overlap
blocks.body: The s orbital of one H atom overlaps with the s orbital of another H atom (head-on). Forms σ bond in H₂ molecule.
items: Electron density is symmetrical around both nuclei
H₂ molecule is non-polar (both atoms identical)
Electrons equally distributed between two nuclei
blocks.note: Both s orbitals are half-filled (1s¹ each) before overlap.

blocks.caption: s-s overlap forming σ bond in H₂ molecule
blocks.alt: Two circles (s orbitals) merging into elongated oval representing σ bond

blocks.head: s-p Overlap
blocks.body: Half-filled s orbital of one atom overlaps with half-filled p orbital of another. Shown in HCl formation.
items: H: 1s¹ (half-filled s orbital)
Cl: [Ne], 3s², 3p⁴ 3p¹ 3p¹ — has half-filled 3p orbital
s-p overlap → σ bond
Electron density higher near Cl (more electronegative) → HCl is polar

blocks.caption: s-p overlap in HCl — σ bond formation with polarization
blocks.alt: Sphere (H 1s) overlapping with lobe of dumbbell (Cl 3p) along axis

blocks.head: p-p Overlap (Head-on / Linear)
blocks.body: p orbitals of two atoms overlap head-on along the inter-nuclear axis. Example: Cl₂ molecule.
items: Each Cl has half-filled 3p orbital
Head-on overlap → σ bond
Electron density symmetrical (both atoms same EN)

blocks.caption: Head-on p-p overlap forming σ bond in Cl₂
blocks.alt: Two dumbbells facing each other along x-axis, lobes merging

blocks.head: Electron Density in σ Bond
blocks.body: Electron density is between the two nuclei (along inter-nuclear axis). σ bond is a strong bond.
items: Formed by head-on (linear) overlapping
Head-on overlapping → strong overlap → strong bond
Parallel overlapping → weak bond (π bond)

blocks.label: Pi (π) Bond
blocks.text: A π bond is formed by the parallel (sideways) overlapping of two half-filled p orbitals. When two orbitals do parallel overlapping, a pi bond is formed.

blocks.head: π Bond in O₂ (O=O)
blocks.body: Oxygen has two unpaired electrons in perpendicular p orbitals (Pₓ and Pᵧ).
items: O electronic config: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z² (lone pair)
pₓ orbitals: overlap head-on → σ bond
pᵧ orbitals: aligned parallel → overlap above and below the plane → π bond
O₂ has one σ bond + one π bond = double bond (O=O)
Four lobes overlap in π bond: two above plane, two below plane

blocks.caption: Formation of σ and π bonds in O₂ — double bond
blocks.alt: Two oxygen atoms with sigma bond along axis and two pi lobes above and below

blocks.head: Comparing σ and π Bonds
items: σ bond: head-on overlap, electron density along inter-nuclear axis, stronger
π bond: parallel (sideways) overlap, electron density above and below nuclear axis, weaker
σ bond strength > π bond strength
Single bond = 1σ; Double bond = 1σ + 1π; Triple bond = 1σ + 2π

blocks.caption: Comparison: head-on (σ) vs parallel (π) orbital overlap
blocks.alt: Side by side: two dumbbells facing each other for sigma, two dumbbells stacked parallel for pi

blocks.t: Board favourite: 'Explain σ and π bonds with formation and examples.' Mention VBT postulates, then define each bond, give overlap type, electron density position, and example molecule.

blocks.head: Formation of HF Molecule
blocks.body: H (1s¹) makes one bond with F by s-p overlap because each has one half-filled orbital.
items: H: 1s¹
F: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ², 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹ — has half-filled orbital
H makes one bond with F
F is strongly electronegative → attracts bond pair more strongly → polarization
Polarity: H^δ⁺ ··· F^δ⁻

blocks.head: Formation of H₂S Molecule
blocks.body: Sulfur has two half-filled 3p orbitals (3pᵧ and 3p_z), so it makes two bonds with two H atoms.
items: S electronic config: [Ne], 3s², 3pₓ², 3pᵧ¹, 3p_z¹
Two 3p orbitals of S each overlap with 1s of two H atoms
V-shaped (bent) molecule formed
Bond angle: 92° (p orbitals are at 90° — closer to 90° than H₂O)

items.q: Draw the orbital structures of H₂O and N₂ molecules.
items.ans:
H₂O: O has config: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ², 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹. Two half-filled p orbitals each overlap with 1s of two H atoms. Bond angle ~104.5° (lone pairs compress).

N₂: N config: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹. pₓ-pₓ head-on → σ bond; pᵧ-pᵧ and p_z-p_z parallel → two π bonds. Triple bond: N≡N (1σ + 2π).

items.q: Draw the orbital overlap to show the formation of F₂ and HF molecules.
items.ans:
F₂: Each F: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ², 2pᵧ², 2p_z¹. The half-filled p_z orbitals overlap head-on → p-p σ bond. Single bond (F–F).

HF: H (1s¹) + F (half-filled 2p) → s-p overlap → σ bond. Electron density shifts toward F (higher EN).

blocks.label: Hybridization
blocks.text: A process in which atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes are mixed together to form a new set of equivalent orbitals of same energy and same shape is called hybridization.

blocks.head: Key Points (Keep in Mind)
items: Hybridization is mixing of orbitals in a single atom (not between two atoms)
Only orbitals of comparable (close) energies can mix
Number of hybrid orbitals = number of mixing orbitals
Conditions: orbitals must have little energy difference; same shell number; proper energy for excitation of electrons

blocks.head: Why Hybridization Happens
blocks.body: s-orbital is spherical with low energy. p-orbital is dumb-bell shaped with high energy. They intermix to form equivalent hybrid orbitals of intermediate energy and shape. The hybrid orbitals can make stronger bonds than unhybridized orbitals.

blocks.label: sp Hybridization
blocks.text: Intermixing of one 's' and one 'p' orbital of different shape and energy to form two degenerate sp orbitals is called sp hybridization.

blocks.head: sp Hybridization — Details
blocks.body: Two sp hybrid orbitals are formed. They are linear and oriented at 180°.
items: Mixing: 1s + 1p → 2 sp hybrid orbitals
Geometry: Linear
Bond angle: 180°
Examples: BeCl₂, CH≡CH (acetylene)
s-orbital: spherical, low energy; p-orbital: dumb-bell, high energy
blocks.eq:
Be ground state:  2s² 2p⁰ 2p⁰ 2p⁰
Be excited state: 2s¹ 2p¹ 2p⁰ 2p⁰
Be hybridized:    sp   sp  (two degenerate sp orbitals)

blocks.caption: sp hybridization — energy diagram and two sp orbitals at 180°
blocks.alt: Energy diagram showing 2s and 2p combining to form two sp orbitals; orbital diagram showing two lobes at 180 degrees

blocks.head: BeCl₂ (sp hybridized)
blocks.body: Beryllium chloride is the classic sp example.
items: Be electronic config: 1s², 2s²
Be excited: 1s², 2s¹, 2p¹ — two half-filled orbitals
sp hybridization → two sp orbitals
Two sp hybrid orbitals of Be overlap with half-filled p-orbitals of two Cl atoms
sp–p linear overlapping forms σ bond
Formula: Cl — Be — Cl (linear)

blocks.label: sp² Hybridization
blocks.text: Intermixing of one 's' and two 'p' orbitals of different shape and energy to form three degenerate sp² orbitals is called sp² hybridization.

blocks.head: sp² Hybridization — Details
blocks.body: Three sp² hybrid orbitals are formed, arranged in a trigonal planar geometry.
items: Mixing: 1s + 2p → 3 sp² hybrid orbitals
Geometry: Trigonal Planar
Bond angle: 120°
Examples: BF₃, alkenes (CH₂=CH₂), carbonyl group (C=O)
blocks.eq:
B ground state:  2s² 2p¹ 2p⁰ 2p⁰
B excited state: 2s¹ 2p¹ 2p¹ 2p⁰
B hybridized:    sp²  sp²  sp²

blocks.caption: sp² hybridization — energy diagram and three sp² orbitals at 120°
blocks.alt: Energy diagram showing s + two p orbitals combining; three orbital lobes pointing 120 degrees apart in a plane

blocks.head: Boron Trifluoride — BF₃ (sp² example)
blocks.body: BF₃ is the standard example for sp² hybridization.
items: B electronic config: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ⁰, 2p_z⁰
B excited: 1s², 2s¹, 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹ — three half-filled orbitals
Three outermost orbitals mix → three sp² hybrid orbitals
B has three half-filled sp² orbitals so it makes three bonds
Each sp² of B overlaps with half-filled 2p_z of F → σ bond
BF₃: trigonal planar, bond angle 120°
9F config: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ², 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹ → uses one half-filled p orbital for bonding

blocks.caption: BF₃ trigonal planar structure with sp² hybridized B at center
blocks.alt: B in center, three F atoms at 120 degree angles, flat triangular shape

blocks.label: sp³ Hybridization
blocks.text: Intermixing of one 's' and three 'p' orbitals of different energy and shape to form four degenerate sp³ orbitals is called sp³ hybridization.

blocks.head: sp³ Hybridization — Details
blocks.body: Four sp³ hybrid orbitals are formed, arranged in a tetrahedral geometry.
items: Mixing: 1s + 3p → 4 sp³ hybrid orbitals
Geometry: Tetrahedral
Bond angle: 109.5°
Examples: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, alkanes, H₃O⁺
blocks.eq:
C ground state: 2s² 2pₓ¹ 2pᵧ¹ 2p_z⁰
C excited:      2s¹ 2pₓ¹ 2pᵧ¹ 2p_z¹
C hybridized:   sp³  sp³  sp³  sp³

blocks.caption: sp³ hybridization — energy diagram and four sp³ orbitals in tetrahedral arrangement
blocks.alt: Energy diagram: 2s + three 2p → four sp3 orbitals; tetrahedral shape with 109.5 degree angles

blocks.head: Methane CH₄ (sp³ example)
blocks.body: Methane is the classic sp³ example. Central atom: C.
items: C config (ground): 1s², 2s², 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z⁰
C excited: 2s¹, 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹ — four half-filled orbitals
Four orbitals mix → four sp³ hybrid orbitals
Each sp³ of C overlaps with 1s of four H atoms → four σ bonds
Four C-H bonds directed to corners of regular tetrahedron
Bond angle: 109.5°

blocks.head: Did You Know?
blocks.body: Each sp³ hybrid orbital has two lobes — one large and one small. For simplicity, the smaller lobe is usually not shown in diagrams.

blocks.t: For board exams: memorize the 3 types: sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°). Always mention the mixing (1s+1p, 1s+2p, 1s+3p), the number of hybrid orbitals formed, geometry, bond angle, and example.

sections.title: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Model (VSEPR)

blocks.label: VSEPR Theory
blocks.text: The VSEPR model describes the shapes of molecules based on the electron pairs that surround the central atom. It is based on the assumption that a molecule will take a shape such that the electronic repulsions among the valence electron pairs of that atom are minimum.

blocks.head: Origin
blocks.body: VSEPR theory was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940.
blocks.note: Full form: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Theory

blocks.head: Importance
blocks.body: It explains the shape and geometry of a molecule based on the electron pairs that surround the central atom. In order to minimize repulsion, electron pairs arrange themselves farthest possible distance apart.

items.title: Contribution of Electrons
items.body: — Both lone pairs (non-bonded) and bond pairs contribute to determine the geometry of molecules.

items.title: Maximum Distance
items.body: — Electron pairs arrange around central atom at maximum distance apart to avoid repulsions.

items.title: Repulsion Order (Space Occupied)
items.body: — Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs. Lone pair causes more repulsion than bond pair. Repulsion order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp

items.title: Presence of Multiple Bonds
items.body: — The two electron pairs of a double bond or three electron pairs of a triple bond contain higher electronic charge density, but they are considered a single electron pair as it is on the same axis.

items.title: Presence of Highly Electronegative Atoms
items.body: — Highly electronegative atoms with the central atom cause: decreased electronic repulsions between bond pairs, but stronger repulsion by the lone pair. Bonds come close and decrease bond angle.

blocks.head: Influence of Nucleus on Pairs
blocks.body: Bond pair electrons are under influence of two nuclei (stronger hold). Lone pair electrons are under influence of only one nucleus (weaker hold — more space occupied, more repulsion).
blocks.note: This is why lone pairs cause more repulsion than bond pairs.

blocks.caption: Comparison of space occupied by lone pair vs bond pair around central atom X
blocks.alt: Two diagrams: left shows H-X with small bond pair region; right shows X lone pair with wider repulsion cloud

blocks.head: Notation System
blocks.body: Central atom = A. Surrounding bonded atoms = B. Lone pairs = L.
items: Total pairs of electrons = (valence e⁻ of central atom + e⁻ shared by surrounding atoms) ÷ 2
Bond angle is found using bond pairs only — not determined by lone pairs
Geometry/shape is determined by bond pairs only
blocks.eq:
Total pairs = [V + M - C + A] ÷ 2
V = valence electrons of central atom
M = monovalent atoms × 1
C = charge (subtract if cation, add if anion)
A = anion electrons (if needed)

blocks.head: Steps to Find Shape
items: Step 1 — Determine central atom (least electronegative or least number of atoms, e.g. Be in BeCl₂, B in BF₃)
Step 2 — Calculate electron pairs around central atom (bond + lone pairs)
Step 3 — Determine electron pair geometry from total pairs
Step 4 — Determine actual shape excluding lone pairs
Example: In CCl₄ → C has 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral shape

blocks.head: How to Calculate Lone Pairs
blocks.body: Example using NH₃:
blocks.eq:
Valence electrons of N = 5
Electrons shared by 3H = 3 × 1 = 3
Total electrons = 5 + 3 = 8
Total pairs = 8 ÷ 2 = 4
Lone pairs = Total pairs - Bond pairs = 4 - 3 = 1
∴ N has 1 lone pair in NH₃

blocks.t: Board exam tip: always state electron pair geometry first, then actual shape (excluding lone pairs). Mention that lone pairs reduce bond angles.

blocks.head: BeCl₂ — AB₂ (Linear)
blocks.body: Be has 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. Electron pairs at 180° — linear.
items: Electrons around Be = 2 pairs
Bond pair = 2, Lone pair = 0
Shape: Linear
Bond angle: 180°
Examples: BeCl₂, ZnCl₂, CO₂ (multiple bonds treated as one)

blocks.head: BF₃ — AB₃ (Trigonal Planar)
blocks.body: 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. All at 120° in same plane.
items: Total pairs = 3, Bond pair = 3, Lone pair = 0
Shape: Trigonal Planar
Bond angle: 120°
Examples: BF₃, BCl₃, SO₃, AlH₃, GaH₃

blocks.head: SnCl₂ — AB₃ with One Lone Pair (V-shaped)
blocks.body: Sn has 4 electrons in outermost shell. Makes 2 bonds with Cl. Remaining 2 electrons = 1 lone pair.
items: Bond pair = 2, Lone pair = 1
Electron pair geometry: Trigonal
Actual shape: V-shaped (angular)
Bond angle: less than 120° (lone pair repulsion)
Similarly: SO₂ has 1 lone pair and 2 double bonds (S=O) → V-shaped

blocks.head: CH₄ — AB₄ (Tetrahedral)
blocks.body: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. Regular tetrahedron.
items: Total pairs = (4+4)/2 = 4, Bond pair = 4, Lone pair = 0
Shape: Tetrahedral
Bond angle: 109.5°
Examples: CH₄, SiH₄, GeCl₄, CCl₄

blocks.caption: CH₄ regular tetrahedral shape with 109.5° bond angles
blocks.alt: Carbon in center with 4 hydrogen atoms at tetrahedral corners, 109.5 degree angles shown

blocks.head: NH₃ — AB₄ with One Lone Pair (Trigonal Pyramidal)
blocks.body: 3 bond pairs, 1 lone pair. Lone pair reduces bond angle.
items: Total pairs = (5+3)/2 = 4, Bond pair = 3, Lone pair = 1
Electron pair geometry: Tetrahedral
Actual shape: Trigonal Pyramidal (distorted tetrahedral)
Bond angle: reduced from 109.5° to 107°
H₃O⁺ ion: same type, also trigonal pyramidal (bond angle ~107°)

blocks.head: NF₃ — Bond Angle further reduced (102.5°)
blocks.body: In NF₃, N is bonded to highly electronegative F atoms. Two effects:
items: Strong polarity of N-F bond → N pulls lone pair closer to its nucleus
Lone pair exerts stronger repulsion on bond pairs
Bond pairs (N-F) are closer to F than N → increased distance → weaker bp-bp repulsion
Bond angle compressed further to 102.5°

blocks.head: H₂O — AB₄ with Two Lone Pairs (V-shaped)
blocks.body: 2 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs. Greater repulsion from two lone pairs.
items: Total pairs = (6+2)/2 = 4, Bond pair = 2, Lone pair = 2
Electron pair geometry: Tetrahedral
Actual shape: V-shaped (angular/bent)
Bond angle: 104.5° (reduced from 109.5° by two lone pairs)
Two corners of tetrahedron occupied by O-H bonds; other two by lone pairs

blocks.caption: H₂O: tetrahedral electron pair geometry vs actual V-shaped molecular shape
blocks.alt: Left: tetrahedral with two lone pairs and two O-H bonds; Right: V-shaped structure with 104.5 degree angle

blocks.head: H₃O⁺ (Hydronium Ion) — Trigonal Pyramidal
blocks.body: H₃O⁺ is formed by capture of a proton by a water molecule.
items: Electron pair = (5+3)/2 = 4 (note: +1 charge removes one electron → use 5+3-1+1=8? See calc below)
Total e⁻ pairs around O = (6+3-1)/2 = 4 (O valence 6, 3H × 1, -1 for +charge)
Bond pair = 3, Lone pair = 1
Shape: Trigonal Pyramidal
Bond angle: 107° (reduced by one lone pair)
blocks.eq:
Electron pairs = (V + M - charge) / 2
= (5 + 3 - (-1)) / 2 ... wait: H₃O⁺
O: V=6, 3H shared, charge = +1 (subtract)
= (6 + 3 - 1) / 2 = 8/2 = 4 pairs

blocks.head: PCl₅ — AB₅ (Trigonal Bipyramidal)
blocks.body: 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. Two types of positions: axial and equatorial.
items: Electron pair = (5+5)/2 = 5, Bond pair = 5, Lone pair = 0
Shape: Trigonal Bipyramidal
Two electron pairs are axial (above and below plane)
Three electron pairs are in trigonal planar (equatorial plane)
Bond angle: within plane 120°; between planar and axial 90°

blocks.caption: PCl₅ trigonal bipyramidal shape — 3 equatorial (120°) + 2 axial bonds
blocks.alt: P in center with 3 Cl in equatorial plane at 120 degrees and 2 Cl above and below at 90 degrees

blocks.head: I₃⁻ (Tri-iodide Ion) — AB₅ type with 3 Lone Pairs (Linear)
blocks.body: I₃⁻ is formed by combination of I₂ and I⁻. Central I has 5 pairs total.
items: Electron pairs = (7+3)/2 = 5 around central I
Bond pair = 2 (axial positions), Lone pair = 3 (equatorial positions)
Geometry: Trigonal Bipyramidal
Actual shape: Linear (lone pairs occupy equatorial corners)
Bond angle: 180°

blocks.head: SF₆ — AB₆ (Octahedral)
blocks.body: 6 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. All angles 90°.
items: Electron pair = 6, Bond pair = 6, Lone pair = 0
Shape: Octahedral
Bond angle: 90°

blocks.head: XeF₄ — AB₆ with 2 Lone Pairs (Square Planar)
blocks.body: 4 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs. Two lone pairs occupy axial positions.
items: Electron pair = (8+4)/2 = 6, Bond pair = 4, Lone pair = 2
Geometry: Octahedral
Two lone pairs stay farthest apart at 180° (axial positions)
Four bond pairs in equatorial plane
Actual shape: Square Planar
Bond angle: 90°

blocks.caption: XeF₄ square planar shape — 2 lone pairs axial, 4 F in equatorial plane
blocks.alt: Xe in center, 4 F atoms at 90 degrees in square plane, 2 lone pairs above and below

blocks.t: 3.8.2 Applications of VSEPR in Drug Design

blocks.label: Drugs
blocks.text: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose, or treat a disease.

blocks.head: Key Terms in Drug Action
items: Substrate (Target): Part of body or any process on which the drug acts is called substrate.
Ligands: Bioactive sites of a medicine are called ligands.
Receptor: It is usually a protein that receives and responds to a ligand by binding process.
Specificity: Each drug interacts with a different substrate at a different degree — this is called specificity.
Examples of substrates: stomach, blood pressure

blocks.head: Lock and Key Model
blocks.body: VSEPR theory explains the action of drugs in lock and key model. Only ligands with suitable shape can fit in the active sites of a biological target — like a specific key fits a specific lock.
items: According to this, a specific key can open a specific lock
Each drug has a specific bioactive site
In similar way, each drug has specific bioactive sites — drug shape must match receptor shape
VSEPR is applied in determining shapes of biological systems such as substrate recognition, ligand specificity, antibody recognition

blocks.head: Example: Aspirin (Acetyl-Salicylate)
blocks.body: Aspirin is an analgesic drug (painkiller) used for relief from pain.
items: Active site: –OCCH₃ (acetyl group)
Aspirin's active site (CH₃CO) matches with COX (cyclooxygenase enzyme)
Higher COX causes pain in body
Acetyl group combines with COX and decreases its action
Shape of COX active site is compatible with acetyl group on Aspirin → binding blocks COX

blocks.head: Limitations of VSEPR
items: Does not explain formation of bonds
Does not explain direction of bond
Does not explain strength of bond
Does not explain paramagnetic behaviour

items.q: Calculate the no. of lone pairs on the central atoms in H₂O, ICl₃, I₃⁻.
items.ans:
H₂O: Total pairs = (6+2)/2 = 4; Bond pairs = 2; Lone pairs = 2.

ICl₃: Total pairs = (7+3)/2 = 5; Bond pairs = 3; Lone pairs = 2.

I₃⁻: Total pairs = (7+3+1)/2 = 5 (extra e for negative charge); Bond pairs = 2; Lone pairs = 3.

items.q: Calculate bond pairs and lone pairs in SiH₄, H₂Se, and PH₃.
items.ans:
SiH₄: Total = (4+4)/2 = 4; Bond = 4; Lone = 0.

H₂Se: Total = (6+2)/2 = 4; Bond = 2; Lone = 2.

PH₃: Total = (5+3)/2 = 4; Bond = 3; Lone = 1.

items.q: Predict the shapes and angles in SiH₄, H₂Se, and PH₃.
items.ans:
SiH₄: Tetrahedral; bond angle 109.5° (Si in Group IVA, same as CH₄).

H₂Se: V-shaped; bond angle less than 109.5° due to 2 lone pairs and larger size of Se orbital (actually ~91°).

PH₃: Trigonal pyramidal; bond angle less than 109.5° due to 1 lone pair repulsion.

items.q: How would the bond angle in H₂S differ from H₂O?
items.ans: H₂S bond angle (92°) is less than H₂O (104.5°). Reason: S orbitals are larger than O orbitals. The two 3p orbitals of S are at 90° to each other. The lone pair on S exerts stronger repulsion due to larger orbital size and greater S-H bond length, pushing bond pairs closer. So H₂S has a smaller bond angle than H₂O.

blocks.label: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)
blocks.text: All the atomic orbitals try to overlap and form molecular orbitals. The molecular orbital approach explains the results of quantum mechanical calculations for covalent bonding.

blocks.head: Postulates of MOT
items: Overlapping of Orbitals: Atomic orbitals (AOs) overlap to form molecular orbitals (MOs). MOs are property of whole molecule.
Types of MOs: MOs are of two types — i) Bonding Molecular Orbital (BMO), ii) Anti-bonding Molecular Orbital (ABMO)
Energy: Energy of anti-bonding MO > Energy of bonding MO. BMOs are at lower energy; ABMOs at high energy.
Filling: Always fill low energy orbitals first (Aufbau principle applies).

blocks.head: Types of MOs
items: Bonding MO (BMO/σ or π): Formed when lobes of same sign overlap (constructive interference). Electron density MAXIMUM between two nuclei. Lower energy.
Anti-bonding MO (ABMO/σ* or π*): Formed when lobes of opposite sign overlap (destructive interference). Electron density MINIMUM (zero at nodal plane) between nuclei. Higher energy.

blocks.caption: Formation of BMO and ABMO from two atomic orbitals — constructive and destructive interference
blocks.alt: Two s orbitals: same sign combining to form BMO (egg shape between nuclei); opposite signs forming ABMO (two separate lobes with node)

blocks.head: Sign Conventions in Wave Functions
blocks.body: In orbitals, wave function is represented as +ve and -ve (ψ). Two lobes overlapping with:
items: Similar sign (+ with +) → BMO (constructive overlap)
Dissimilar sign (+ with –) → ABMO (destructive overlap)

blocks.label: Bond Order (B.O.)
blocks.text: The number of bonds between two atoms is called bond order. It is calculated as half of the difference between electrons in bonding MOs and electrons in anti-bonding MOs.

blocks.t:
Bond Order (B.O.) = (electrons in BMOs - electrons in ABMOs) / 2

             a - b
B.O.  =  ─────────
               2

where a = electrons in BMOs
      b = electrons in ABMOs

blocks.head: Paramagnetic Behaviour
blocks.body: If molecular orbitals have unpaired electrons then molecule is paramagnetic. If no unpaired electrons, then molecule is diamagnetic.
items: Unpaired electrons → paramagnetic (attracted weakly by magnet)
No unpaired electrons → diamagnetic
O₂: paramagnetic (two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals) — liquid O₂ attracted by magnet
N₂: diamagnetic (all electrons paired)

blocks.head: s-s Overlap → σ and σ*
blocks.body: Two s orbitals of atoms combine to give two molecular orbitals.
items: Same sign overlap → σ (1s) bonding MO — electron density along inter-nuclear axis
Opposite sign overlap → σ* (1s) anti-bonding MO — electron density away from nuclei
Electrons of bonding MO are along inter-nuclear axis

blocks.head: Head-on (Linear) p-p Overlap
blocks.body: p orbitals along the same axis (say x-axis) approach each other head-on.
items: Electron density of BMO is maximum between two nuclei
Gives: σ(2pₓ) bonding and σ*(2pₓ) antibonding MOs
Electron of π-BMO is zero between inter-molecular axis — present above and below the plane

blocks.head: Parallel (Sideways) p-p Overlap
blocks.body: When pᵧ or p_z orbitals are parallel to each other, they interact to form π MOs.
items: BMO: π(2pᵧ) or π(2p_z) — zero electron density on nuclear axis (nodal plane)
ABMO: π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z) — minimum electron density in inter-nuclear region
Electrons of ABMO are minimum at nodal plane (both π and σ)

blocks.caption: Head-on p-p overlap (σ MOs) and parallel p-p overlap (π MOs)
blocks.alt: Two diagrams: top shows two p orbitals along axis combining to sigma MO; bottom shows parallel p orbitals combining to pi MO above and below plane

blocks.head: Formation of H₂ Molecule
blocks.body: Atomic Number of H = 1. Electron Configuration: 1s¹
items: Two 1s orbitals (one from each H) combine → σ(1s) and σ*(1s)
2 electrons fill the lower energy σ(1s) BMO
MO configuration: (σ1s)²
Bond Order = (2-0)/2 = 1 → single bond H–H
Always fill low energy orbital first
H₂ is diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons)

blocks.caption: MO diagram of H₂ — 2 electrons in σ(1s) BMO
blocks.alt: Energy level diagram: two 1s AOs on sides, σ*1s ABMO at top center (empty), σ1s BMO at bottom center (2 electrons)

blocks.head: Formation of He₂ Molecule
blocks.body: Atomic Number of He = 2. Electron Configuration: 1s²
items: Two 1s² orbitals combine → σ(1s) and σ*(1s)
4 electrons: 2 in σ(1s) BMO and 2 in σ*(1s) ABMO
MO config: (σ1s)² (σ*1s)²
Bond Order = (2-2)/2 = 0 → He₂ does NOT exist
blocks.eq:
Bond Order of He₂ = (2 - 2) / 2 = 0
∴ He₂ does not exist

blocks.caption: MO diagram of He₂ — bond order = 0, molecule does not exist
blocks.alt: Energy level diagram: 1s AOs on sides; σ*1s with 2 electrons; σ1s with 2 electrons — equal bonding/antibonding

blocks.head: Formation of N₂ Molecule
blocks.body: Electronic configuration of N: ₇N: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ¹, 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹
items: Energy order of MOs for N₂: σ2s < σ*2s < π2pᵧ = π2p_z < σ2pₓ < π*2pᵧ = π*2p_z < σ*2pₓ
Note: For N₂, π2p comes before σ2pₓ (different from O₂ and F₂)
Total electrons in N₂: 14 → fill all MOs up to σ2pₓ
blocks.eq:
MO config of N₂:
(σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(π2pᵧ)²(π2p_z)²(σ2pₓ)²

Bond Order = (8 - 2) / 2 = 6/2 = 3
∴ N≡N triple bond (1σ + 2π)

blocks.caption: MO diagram of N₂ showing 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons — bond order 3
blocks.alt: Full MO energy level diagram for N2: AOs of both N atoms on sides, MOs in center filled from bottom up to sigma 2px

blocks.head: Magnetic Behaviour of N₂
blocks.body: N₂ is diamagnetic. All electrons are paired in its MOs — no unpaired electrons.
blocks.note: Bond order = 3 confirms the N≡N triple bond seen in Lewis structure.

blocks.head: Formation of O₂ Molecule
blocks.body: Electronic configuration of O: ₈O: 1s², 2s², 2pₓ², 2pᵧ¹, 2p_z¹
items: Energy order of MOs for O₂: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pₓ < π2pᵧ = π2p_z < π*2pᵧ = π*2p_z < σ*2pₓ
Note: For O₂ (and F₂), σ2pₓ comes before π2p (opposite to N₂)
Total electrons in O₂: 16 → fills MOs including π* orbitals
blocks.eq:
MO config of O₂:
(σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(σ2pₓ)²(π2pᵧ)²(π2p_z)²(π*2pᵧ)¹(π*2p_z)¹

Bond Order = (8 - 4) / 2 = 4/2 = 2
∴ O=O double bond (1σ + 1π)

blocks.head: Paramagnetic Nature of O₂
blocks.body: O₂ is paramagnetic — this is the great success of MOT. Lewis structure fails to explain this.
items: Two unpaired electrons: one in π*(2pᵧ) and one in π*(2p_z)
Unpaired electrons create net magnetic field
This interacts with external magnetic field → paramagnetic behavior
Liquid O₂ is attracted and suspended between poles of strong magnet
MOT successfully explains paramagnetic nature of O₂ which VSEPR and VBT cannot

blocks.caption: MO diagram of O₂ showing 2 unpaired electrons in π* orbitals — paramagnetic
blocks.alt: Full MO energy level diagram for O2: sigma and pi MOs filled; two pi-star orbitals each with 1 unpaired electron shown

blocks.head: NOTE ERROR — Energy Order
blocks.wrong: Notes write the energy order of N₂ MOs as: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pₓ < π2pᵧ = π2p_z which is the O₂ order
blocks.correct: For N₂: π2pᵧ = π2p_z comes BEFORE σ2pₓ in the energy order. For O₂ and F₂: σ2pₓ comes before π2pᵧ.
blocks.reason: Notes appear to use O₂ energy order for N₂. These are different. N₂ energy order: σ2s < σ*2s < π2pᵧ = π2p_z < σ2pₓ. O₂ energy order: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pₓ < π2pᵧ = π2p_z.

blocks.t: Board exam: When asked about paramagnetic nature of O₂ — state that MOT shows O₂ has two unpaired electrons in π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z). This gives it a net magnetic field. Liquid O₂ is attracted by a magnet. This is not explained by Lewis structure.

items.q: Draw Lewis structures for IF₃ and IF₅ and predict their geometry with reference to the VSEPR model.
items.ans:
IF₃: I has 7 valence e⁻, 3 F contribute 3 e⁻. Total pairs = (7+3)/2 = 5. Bond pairs = 3, Lone pairs = 2. Electron pair geometry: Trigonal Bipyramidal. Actual shape: T-shaped. Bond angle: 90° (axial F) and ~87° (modified by lone pairs).

IF₅: I has 7 valence e⁻, 5 F contribute 5 e⁻. Total pairs = (7+5)/2 = 6. Bond pairs = 5, Lone pairs = 1. Electron pair geometry: Octahedral. Actual shape: Square Pyramidal. Bond angles: ~90°.

mcqs.q: Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment?
mcqs.exp: BF₃ is trigonal planar and perfectly symmetrical. The three B-F bond moments cancel each other out. Net dipole moment = 0. NH₃, CHCl₃ and H₂O are all unsymmetrical and have non-zero dipole moments.

mcqs.q: The numbers of σ and π bonds in the N₂ molecule are:
opts: One σ and one π bonds
One σ and two π bonds
mcqs.exp: N₂ has a triple bond (N≡N). Triple bond = 1σ + 2π. The σ bond forms from head-on overlap of 2pₓ orbitals; the two π bonds from parallel overlap of 2pᵧ and 2p_z orbitals.

mcqs.q: Which of the following species has unpaired electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals?
mcqs.exp: O₂²⁺ has 14 electrons (removed 2 from O₂). MO filling leaves unpaired electrons in antibonding π* orbitals. Regular O₂ has 2 unpaired electrons in π*; O₂²⁺ has fewer total electrons but still has unpaired electrons in ABMO.

mcqs.q: The shape of ICl₅ according to the VSEPR model is:
mcqs.exp: Wait — ICl₅: I has 7 valence e⁻ + 5 from Cl = 12 total → 6 pairs. Bond pairs = 5, Lone pairs = 1. Electron pair geometry: Octahedral. Actual shape: Square Pyramidal. However the book answer listed here is Trigonal Bipyramidal which would be for AB₅ with no lone pair like PCl₅. ICl₅ is actually Square Pyramidal (AB₅ with 1LP in octahedral geometry).
mcqs.note_error: The book option 'Trigonal bipyramidal' for ICl₅ is incorrect if referring to shape (should be Square Pyramidal). Trigonal bipyramidal is the electron pair geometry of PCl₅ which has 0 lone pairs.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are present in the valence shell of P in PO₄³⁻?
mcqs.exp: P in PO₄³⁻ has expanded octet. Valence electrons = 2×(no. of double bonds) + 2×(no. of single bonds). In PO₄³⁻, P forms 4 bonds. Counting: 2×4 (double) + 2×4 (single) or calculating from Lewis structure → 12 electrons around P. This exceeds octet by 4.

mcqs.q: How many extra electrons than a normal octet are there in the valence shell of I in ICl₅?
mcqs.exp: ICl₅: I forms 5 bonds + 1 lone pair = 6 pairs = 12 electrons in valence shell. Normal octet = 8. Extra = 12 - 8 = 4. Wait — the answer 2 would mean 10 electrons. Let me recalculate: if we mean extra pairs, 5 bond pairs + 1 LP = 6 pairs. 6 pairs = 12 e⁻. Octet = 8. Extra = 4. Answer should be C (4).
mcqs.note_error: Review this calculation carefully in exam.

mcqs.q: What is the type and shape of [ICl₄]⁻ according to the VSEPR model?
mcqs.exp: [ICl₄]⁻: I has 7 valence e⁻, 4 Cl contribute 4 e⁻, plus 1 for negative charge = 12 total → 6 pairs. Bond pairs = 4, Lone pairs = 2. Electron pair geometry = Octahedral → actual shape = Square Planar. Type = AB₆ system.

mcqs.q: Which of the following molecules has a central atom with sp³ hybridization and a tetrahedral electron pair geometry?
mcqs.exp: CCl₄: C is sp³ hybridized. 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → regular tetrahedral geometry with 109.5° angles. BF₃ is sp² (trigonal planar). SO₂ has sp² central S. PCl₅ is sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal).

mcqs.q: In which molecule does MOT predict paramagnetic behavior that Lewis structure cannot explain?
mcqs.exp: O₂ is predicted to be paramagnetic by MOT because the MO diagram shows 2 unpaired electrons in degenerate π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z) orbitals. The Lewis structure of O₂ (O=O) shows all electrons paired, which is incorrect. This is one of the greatest successes of MOT.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridization of the central atom in BeCl₂?
mcqs.exp: BeCl₂: Be has 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → linear geometry, bond angle 180°. This corresponds to sp hybridization (1s + 1p → 2 sp orbitals). Linear geometry always indicates sp hybridization.

mcqs.q: Bond order of He₂ molecule is:
mcqs.exp: He₂: each He has 1s². Two He atoms combine → 4 electrons fill σ(1s)² and σ*(1s)². Bond Order = (2-2)/2 = 0. Since B.O. = 0, He₂ does not exist.

mcqs.q: Which type of bond is formed by parallel overlap of two p orbitals?
mcqs.exp: π (pi) bond is formed by parallel (sideways) overlap of two p orbitals. The lobes overlap above and below the internuclear axis. σ bonds are formed by head-on (linear) overlap.

mcqs.q: The actual shape of the water molecule (H₂O) is:
mcqs.exp: H₂O has 4 electron pairs (tetrahedral electron pair geometry) but 2 are lone pairs. Excluding lone pairs, the actual shape is V-shaped (angular/bent) with bond angle 104.5°. It would be tetrahedral if all 4 pairs were bond pairs.

sqs.q: Xenon trioxide (XeO₃) structure: By counting electron pairs around the central atom, explain why xenon trioxide has a pyramidal shape. Draw structure showing partial charges and dipole moment direction.
sqs.a:
Electron pair calculation for XeO₃:

Xe valence electrons = 8; 3 oxygen atoms contribute 3×2 = 6 (treating each O as double-bonded). Total electron pairs around Xe = (8 + 0 — for double bonds counted as single) → 4 pairs total (3 bond regions + 1 lone pair).

Shape: Xe has 4 electron pairs: 3 bond pairs (Xe=O double bonds each counted once) and 1 lone pair. This gives trigonal pyramidal shape (same as NH₃ type — AB₄ with 1LP). Bond angle <109.5°.

Dipole moment: The lone pair on Xe plus the polar Xe=O bonds (O is more electronegative) means dipole moments do NOT cancel. The molecule is polar. Dipole moment points from Xe toward the O-rich side (from positive to negative end). Xe carries partial positive charge (δ+); each O carries partial negative charge (δ–).

sqs.q: Explain the difference between the formation of σ (sigma) and π (pi) bonds in terms of VBT.
sqs.a:
σ (Sigma) Bond:

  • Formation: Formed by linear (head-on) overlap of two half-filled orbitals along the inter-nuclear axis.
  • Types of overlap: s-s, s-p, or p-p (head-on).
  • Electron density: Maximum between the two nuclei, along inter-nuclear axis.
  • Strength: σ bond is stronger than π bond (greater overlap).
  • Example: H–H bond in H₂ (s-s overlap); H–Cl in HCl (s-p overlap).

π (Pi) Bond:

  • Formation: Formed by parallel (sideways) overlap of two half-filled p orbitals.
  • Electron density: Above and below the inter-nuclear axis (not between nuclei). Zero at nodal plane.
  • Strength: Weaker than σ bond (less overlap in parallel orientation).
  • Example: O₂ has one π bond (along with one σ bond). N₂ has two π bonds.

Conclusion: Single bond = 1σ; Double bond = 1σ + 1π; Triple bond = 1σ + 2π.

sqs.q: The structure of propanone (acetone) is H₃C–C(=O)–CH₃. (i) Show how the central carbon atom forms σ and π bonds through hybridization. (ii) Can propanone make a hydrogen bond with water?
sqs.a:
(i) Hybridization of central C in propanone:

The central carbon (carbonyl carbon, C=O) is sp² hybridized. This is because:

  • C forms 3 sigma bonds: one to each CH₃ group and involved in C=O.
  • sp² hybridization → 3 sp² orbitals arranged trigonally (120°) + 1 unhybridized p orbital.
  • The 3 sp² orbitals form σ bonds (head-on overlap) with the two CH₃ carbons and with O.
  • The unhybridized p orbital overlaps in parallel with a p orbital on O → π bond.
  • Result: C=O double bond = 1σ + 1π.

(ii) Hydrogen bonding with water:

Yes, propanone can form hydrogen bonds with water. Propanone has a polar C=O group. The lone pairs on the oxygen of C=O can accept an H-bond from water (H–O–H). However, propanone itself cannot donate an H-bond (no O-H or N-H group). So propanone acts as H-bond acceptor with water. This is why propanone (acetone) is miscible with water.

sqs.q: Predict the shapes of sulfate [SO₄]²⁻, borate [BH₄]⁻ and tri-iodide [I₃]⁻ ions according to the VSEPR model.
sqs.a:
[SO₄]²⁻ (Sulfate):

  • S valence e⁻ = 6; 4 oxygen atoms; charge = 2– (add 2 e⁻)
  • Total pairs = (6 + 0 + 2) ÷ 2 = 4 (treating as 4 S-O bonds)
  • Bond pairs = 4; Lone pairs = 0
  • Shape: Tetrahedral; Bond angle: 109.5°
  • Note: S has expanded octet with 12 electrons (involves d orbitals)

[BH₄]⁻ (Borate):

  • B valence e⁻ = 3; 4 H atoms; charge = 1– (add 1 e⁻)
  • Total pairs = (3 + 4 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4
  • Bond pairs = 4; Lone pairs = 0
  • Shape: Tetrahedral; Bond angle: 109.5°

[I₃]⁻ (Tri-iodide):

  • Central I valence e⁻ = 7; 2 I atoms contribute 2; charge = 1– (add 1)
  • Total pairs = (7 + 2 + 1) ÷ 2 = 5
  • Bond pairs = 2; Lone pairs = 3
  • Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal geometry
  • Shape: Linear; Bond angle: 180°

sqs.q: Sketch the molecular orbital pictures of π(2p) and π*(2p).
sqs.a:
π(2p) — Bonding Pi MO:

  • Formed when two parallel p orbitals overlap with same sign (constructive interference)
  • Electron density is present above and below the inter-nuclear axis
  • Zero electron density on the inter-nuclear axis (nodal plane between atoms)
  • Lower energy than parent atomic orbitals
  • Shaped like two banana-like lobes: one above and one below the molecular axis

π*(2p) — Anti-bonding Pi MO:

  • Formed when two parallel p orbitals overlap with opposite signs (destructive interference)
  • There is a nodal plane perpendicular to the inter-nuclear axis AND a nodal plane along the axis
  • Two lobes on each atom but with a node between them
  • Higher energy than parent atomic orbitals
  • Electrons in π* destabilize the bond

sqs.q: Sketch the hybrid orbitals and bond formation in PCl₃, SiCl₄, and NH₄⁺.
sqs.a:
PCl₃ (sp³ hybridized):

  • P config: [Ne] 3s², 3p³ → excited to 3s¹, 3p³ (3 half-filled p orbitals + 1 lone pair after hybridization)
  • sp³ hybridization → 4 sp³ orbitals: 3 bond with Cl, 1 has lone pair
  • Shape: Trigonal Pyramidal; Bond angle: ~107° (lone pair reduces from 109.5°)
  • 3 σ bonds (sp³–p overlap) with 3 Cl atoms

SiCl₄ (sp³ hybridized):

  • Si config: [Ne] 3s², 3p² → excited to 3s¹, 3p³ (4 half-filled orbitals)
  • sp³ hybridization → 4 equivalent sp³ orbitals, all half-filled
  • 4 σ bonds with 4 Cl atoms (sp³–p overlap)
  • Shape: Regular Tetrahedral; Bond angle: 109.5°; No lone pair

NH₄⁺ (sp³ hybridized):

  • N in NH₃ is sp³; NH₃ donates lone pair to H⁺ (dative bond)
  • All 4 sp³ orbitals of N now involved in bonds (3 N-H bonds + 1 dative N→H bond)
  • NH₄⁺: sp³, 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs
  • Shape: Regular Tetrahedral; Bond angle: 109.5°

sqs.q: Draw the orbital structure of the CO₂ molecule in terms of VBT.
sqs.a:
CO₂ orbital structure (VBT):

Central atom: C. CO₂ has structure: O=C=O (linear, 180°).

Carbon hybridization: sp (linear) — 1s + 1p → 2 sp orbitals at 180°. Two unhybridized p orbitals (pᵧ and p_z) remain.

Bond formation:

  • Each sp orbital of C overlaps head-on with a half-filled p orbital of O → 2 σ bonds (one on each side)
  • The unhybridized pᵧ of C overlaps in parallel with pᵧ of left O → π bond
  • The unhybridized p_z of C overlaps in parallel with p_z of right O → π bond

Result: CO₂ = O=C=O; two C=O double bonds (each = 1σ + 1π); linear shape; bond angle 180°.

O—(sp-p σ)—C—(sp-p σ)—O ↕ pᵧ π ↕ p_z π

sqs.q: Explain VSEPR theory. What are its postulates? Discuss the shape of NH₃ and H₂O with bond angles.
sqs.a:
VSEPR Theory: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory was given by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940. It states that the shape of a molecule depends on the repulsion between electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom. Electron pairs arrange themselves at the maximum distance from each other to minimize repulsion.

Postulates:

  • Both lone pairs and bond pairs determine molecular geometry.
  • Electron pairs arrange at maximum distance apart.
  • Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs → greater repulsion.
  • Repulsion order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp.
  • Multiple bonds (double/triple) are treated as a single pair.

NH₃ (Ammonia):

  • N: 5 valence e⁻; 3 H atoms; Total pairs = 4; Bond pairs = 3; Lone pairs = 1
  • Electron pair geometry: Tetrahedral
  • Actual shape: Trigonal Pyramidal
  • Bond angle: 107° (lone pair pushes bond pairs closer from 109.5°)

H₂O (Water):

  • O: 6 valence e⁻; 2 H atoms; Total pairs = 4; Bond pairs = 2; Lone pairs = 2
  • Electron pair geometry: Tetrahedral
  • Actual shape: V-shaped (angular)
  • Bond angle: 104.5° (two lone pairs cause greater compression)

sqs.q: Explain Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT). Why is O₂ paramagnetic but N₂ is diamagnetic? Calculate bond orders of both.
sqs.a:
Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT):

According to MOT, all atomic orbitals of combining atoms overlap to form molecular orbitals. MOs are property of the entire molecule. Two types of MOs are formed: (i) Bonding MO (BMO) — lower energy, stabilizes bond; (ii) Anti-bonding MO (ABMO) — higher energy, destabilizes bond.

Bond Order formula:

B.O. = (electrons in BMOs - electrons in ABMOs) / 2

O₂ (Paramagnetic):

  • Total electrons = 16
  • MO config: (σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(σ2pₓ)²(π2pᵧ)²(π2p_z)²(π*2pᵧ)¹(π*2p_z)¹
  • BMO electrons = 10; ABMO electrons = 6
  • B.O. = (10-6)/2 = 2 → O=O double bond
  • Two unpaired electrons in π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z) → paramagnetic
  • Liquid O₂ is attracted by magnet

N₂ (Diamagnetic):

  • Total electrons = 14
  • MO config: (σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(π2pᵧ)²(π2p_z)²(σ2pₓ)²
  • BMO electrons = 10; ABMO electrons = 4
  • B.O. = (10-4)/2 = 3 → N≡N triple bond
  • All electrons are paired → diamagnetic

Conclusion: MOT explains the paramagnetic nature of O₂ — a fact that Lewis structure and VSEPR completely fail to explain. This is one of the greatest achievements of MOT.

sqs.q: What is hybridization? Explain sp, sp², and sp³ hybridization with examples and geometries.
sqs.a:
Hybridization: The process of intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes to form a new set of equivalent (degenerate) orbitals of same energy and shape is called hybridization. The number of hybrid orbitals formed equals the number of orbitals mixed.

sp Hybridization:

  • Mixing: 1s + 1p → 2 equivalent sp orbitals
  • Geometry: Linear; Bond angle: 180°
  • Example: BeCl₂ (Cl–Be–Cl), CH≡CH (acetylene)
  • Each sp orbital overlaps with p orbital of Cl → 2 σ bonds

sp² Hybridization:

  • Mixing: 1s + 2p → 3 equivalent sp² orbitals
  • Geometry: Trigonal Planar; Bond angle: 120°
  • Example: BF₃, CH₂=CH₂ (ethene)
  • Three sp² orbitals form 3 σ bonds; unhybridized p orbital forms π bond

sp³ Hybridization:

  • Mixing: 1s + 3p → 4 equivalent sp³ orbitals
  • Geometry: Tetrahedral; Bond angle: 109.5°
  • Example: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O
  • For CH₄: 4 sp³ orbitals each overlap with 1s of 4 H atoms → 4 σ bonds directed to tetrahedral corners

lqs.title: Q6(a) — Chemical Bonding: VBT and Hybridization
lqs.q: Explain Valence Bond Theory (VBT). Describe covalent bonding using the concept of hybridization to describe sp, sp², and sp³ orbitals with examples.

parts.label: VBT — Introduction and Postulates
points: VBT explains: reason for bond formation, strength of bond, and direction of bond
A covalent bond forms when half-filled orbitals of similar energy in valence shells overlap
Greater overlap → stronger bond
Bonds are directional — direction determined by shape and mode of overlapping orbitals
Two types of bonds in VBT: σ (sigma) and π (pi)

parts.label: σ Bond Formation
points: σ bond formed by linear (head-on) overlap along inter-nuclear axis
Types: s-s overlap (H₂), s-p overlap (HCl), p-p head-on (Cl₂)
Electron density maximum between two nuclei
σ bond is a strong bond
Example: s-s overlap in H₂: two 1s¹ orbitals overlap → symmetrical electron density → H–H bond

parts.label: π Bond Formation
points: π bond formed by parallel (sideways) overlap of p orbitals
Electron density above and below inter-nuclear axis (not between nuclei)
π bond is weaker than σ bond
Example: O₂ — pₓ orbitals head-on → σ bond; pᵧ orbitals parallel → π bond → O=O double bond
Single bond = 1σ; Double = 1σ+1π; Triple = 1σ+2π

parts.label: sp Hybridization
points: 1s + 1p → 2 sp hybrid orbitals; Linear geometry; 180° bond angle
Example: BeCl₂ — Be excited state 2s¹ 2p¹; sp hybridization; 2 sp orbitals overlap with Cl p-orbitals
sp orbitals at 180° to each other → linear Cl–Be–Cl

parts.label: sp² Hybridization
points: 1s + 2p → 3 sp² hybrid orbitals; Trigonal planar geometry; 120° bond angle
Example: BF₃ — B excited to 2s¹ 2p¹ 2p¹; three sp² orbitals
Three sp² orbitals of B overlap with p orbitals of 3 F atoms → 3 σ bonds
Remaining unhybridized p orbital can form π bond in other molecules (e.g., alkenes)

parts.label: sp³ Hybridization
points: 1s + 3p → 4 sp³ hybrid orbitals; Tetrahedral geometry; 109.5° bond angle
Example: CH₄ — C excited to 2s¹ 2p³; four sp³ orbitals
Four sp³ orbitals of C overlap with 1s of 4 H atoms → 4 σ bonds directed to corners of tetrahedron
NH₃: 3 bonds + 1 lone pair in sp³ → trigonal pyramidal (107°)
H₂O: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs in sp³ → V-shaped (104.5°)

lqs.title: Q6(a) — Chemical Bonding: VSEPR Theory
lqs.q: State the postulates of VSEPR model. Discuss the shapes of CH₄, NH₃, H₃O⁺, PCl₅, SO₂, and SF₆.

parts.label: Postulates of VSEPR
points: Presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940
Shape determined by electron pairs around central atom — both lone and bond pairs
Electron pairs arrange at maximum distance to minimize repulsion
Repulsion order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp
Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs (under influence of only one nucleus)
Multiple bonds treated as single pair; highly EN atoms cause decreased bp repulsion but stronger lp repulsion

parts.label: CH₄ and NH₃
points: CH₄: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral, 109.5°
NH₃: 4 total pairs (3 bond + 1 lone) → electron geometry tetrahedral; actual shape trigonal pyramidal, 107°
Lone pair in NH₃ reduces angle from 109.5° to 107°

parts.label: H₃O⁺ and SO₂
points: H₃O⁺: same as NH₃ type — 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal, ~107°
SO₂: 3 total pairs (2 S=O bonds + 1 lone pair) → electron geometry trigonal; actual shape V-shaped, <120°
Each S=O double bond counts as one pair in VSEPR

parts.label: PCl₅ and SF₆
points: PCl₅: 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal; angles 120° (equatorial) and 90° (axial)
Three equatorial positions in plane; two axial positions above/below plane
SF₆: 6 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → octahedral; all angles 90°
SF₆ is perfectly symmetrical octahedron

lqs.title: Q6(a) — Chemical Bonding: Molecular Orbital Theory
lqs.q: Explain the salient features of Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT). Draw MO diagrams of H₂, He₂, N₂ and O₂. Calculate bond orders and explain paramagnetic nature of O₂.

parts.label: Salient Features of MOT
points: Atomic orbitals (AOs) overlap to form molecular orbitals (MOs) — property of whole molecule
Two AOs overlap → two MOs: Bonding MO (BMO) at lower energy; Anti-bonding MO (ABMO) at higher energy
BMO: same sign lobes overlap (constructive) — electron density between nuclei
ABMO: opposite sign lobes overlap (destructive) — electron density away from nuclei, nodal plane present
B.O. = (electrons in BMOs − electrons in ABMOs) ÷ 2
Unpaired electrons in MOs → paramagnetic; all paired → diamagnetic

parts.label: H₂ and He₂
points: H₂: 2 electrons in σ(1s) BMO; B.O. = (2-0)/2 = 1 → H–H single bond, diamagnetic
He₂: 4 electrons — 2 in σ(1s) BMO + 2 in σ*(1s) ABMO; B.O. = (2-2)/2 = 0 → He₂ does NOT exist

parts.label: N₂
points: N₂ energy order: σ2s < σ*2s < π2pᵧ = π2p_z < σ2pₓ < π*2pᵧ = π*2p_z < σ*2pₓ
14 electrons fill MOs: BMO e⁻ = 10; ABMO e⁻ = 4
B.O. = (10-4)/2 = 3 → N≡N triple bond (1σ + 2π)
All electrons paired → N₂ is diamagnetic

parts.label: O₂ and Paramagnetic Nature
points: O₂ energy order: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pₓ < π2pᵧ = π2p_z < π*2pᵧ = π*2p_z < σ*2pₓ
16 electrons fill MOs: BMO e⁻ = 10; ABMO e⁻ = 6
B.O. = (10-6)/2 = 2 → O=O double bond (1σ + 1π)
Two unpaired electrons: one each in degenerate π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z)
Unpaired electrons create net magnetic field → O₂ is paramagnetic
Liquid O₂ is attracted and suspended between poles of strong magnet
Lewis structure fails to predict this — MOT's greatest success

quiz.q: Which theory explains the paramagnetic nature of O₂?
quiz.exp: MOT explains paramagnetic nature of O₂ through unpaired electrons in degenerate π*(2pᵧ) and π*(2p_z) antibonding orbitals. Lewis structure (and VSEPR/VBT) fails to show unpaired electrons in O₂.

quiz.q: What is the bond angle in BeCl₂?
quiz.exp: BeCl₂ has sp hybridization. Two sp orbitals are at 180° → linear geometry → bond angle 180°.

quiz.q: In VSEPR theory, repulsion is greatest between:
quiz.exp: Repulsion order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp. Lone pairs are under influence of only one nucleus, occupy more space, and cause greatest repulsion.

quiz.q: Bond order of N₂ molecule is:
quiz.exp: N₂: BMO electrons = 10; ABMO electrons = 4; B.O. = (10-4)/2 = 3. N₂ has a triple bond (N≡N).

quiz.q: Which hybridization explains the trigonal planar shape of BF₃?
quiz.exp: BF₃ has 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → trigonal planar, 120°. This corresponds to sp² hybridization (1s + 2p → 3 sp² orbitals).

quiz.q: Anti-bonding molecular orbital forms when:
quiz.exp: ABMO forms by destructive interference — when lobes of opposite signs (+/−) overlap. This reduces electron density between nuclei and increases energy.

quiz.q: The actual shape of PCl₅ is:
quiz.exp: PCl₅ has 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs. Five pairs arrange in trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Bond angles: 120° (equatorial) and 90° (axial).

quiz.q: In VBT, π bond is formed by:
quiz.exp: π (pi) bond is formed specifically by parallel (sideways) overlap of two p orbitals. The lobes overlap above and below the internuclear axis.

quiz.q: How many lone pairs does the central O in H₂O have?
quiz.exp: H₂O: O valence e⁻ = 6; 2H contribute 2. Total pairs = (6+2)/2 = 4. Bond pairs = 2. Lone pairs = 4 - 2 = 2.

quiz.q: VSEPR theory was presented by:
quiz.exp: VSEPR theory was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940.

quiz.q: Bond order of He₂ is zero because:
opts: equal electrons in BMO and ABMO
quiz.exp: He₂: 4 electrons total → 2 in σ(1s) BMO and 2 in σ*(1s) ABMO. B.O. = (2-2)/2 = 0. Equal bonding and antibonding electrons cancel each other.

quiz.q: Which molecule has trigonal pyramidal shape?
quiz.exp: NH₃ has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair. Electron pair geometry is tetrahedral, but actual shape (excluding lone pair) is trigonal pyramidal with bond angle 107°.

quiz.q: σ bond has electron density:
quiz.exp: In σ bond, electron density is maximum along the inter-nuclear axis between the two nuclei. This is because σ bond forms by head-on (linear) overlap.

quiz.q: What is the shape of XeF₄?
quiz.exp: XeF₄: 6 electron pairs (4 bond + 2 lone). Octahedral electron pair geometry. Two lone pairs in axial positions (180° apart). Four F atoms in square equatorial plane → Square Planar shape.

quiz.q: In sp³ hybridization, how many orbitals are mixed?
quiz.exp: sp³ hybridization mixes 4 orbitals: 1 s-orbital + 3 p-orbitals → 4 equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals of same energy and shape.

quiz.q: The bioactive molecules of a medicine that interact with receptors are called:
quiz.exp: Bioactive sites of a medicine are called ligands. Ligands interact with receptors (usually proteins) through a binding process. Drug specificity depends on how well the ligand shape fits the receptor.

quiz.q: Which of these is the formula for bond order?
quiz.exp: Bond Order = (electrons in BMOs − electrons in ABMOs) / 2, i.e., (a - b) / 2, where a = bonding electrons, b = antibonding electrons.

quiz.q: The shape of I₃⁻ ion is:
quiz.exp: I₃⁻: central I has 5 electron pairs (2 bond + 3 lone). Trigonal bipyramidal electron pair geometry. Three lone pairs occupy equatorial positions; 2 I atoms are in axial positions at 180° → Linear actual shape.

quiz.q: Which overlap gives a stronger bond?
quiz.exp: Head-on (linear) overlap gives a σ bond which is stronger than π bond formed by parallel overlap. Greater overlap in head-on orientation → greater electron density between nuclei → stronger bond.

quiz.q: In the Lock and Key model of drug action, the 'key' represents:
quiz.exp: In the Lock and Key model, the drug ligand (bioactive molecule) acts as the 'key' and the receptor (target protein/enzyme) acts as the 'lock'. Only the ligand with the correct shape fits into the receptor's active site.
